content:
(Hello everyone, a new user here, so I hope I'm posting in the right channel.)

Recently I've been trying out vibe-formalizing complex analysis and related topics, with the goal of eventually amassing enough theorems to start trying to use formalization in topics related to my research. In the process I ended up trying out and developing a workflow where the Lean theorems are annotated with human-readable theorem names, statements and proof sketches. These are then fed to a VS Code extension called Handwave, which uses that metadata in rendering summary articles and dependency graphs etc.

Thus, I'd like to share two GitHub repositories:

  • First, the Handwave extension itself: Handwave
  • Second, my own formalization repository: JJMath

The jjmath repository also serves as a demo of the extension, with various Handwave articles under the handwave/ directory. Unfortunately they are mostly LLM generated at the moment, and therefore quite sloppy, but I still hope it sort of gives you an idea what it looks like if you install the extension and view them through it. My vision is that I'd like to start writing these mostly by hand once I reach my own research problems and the pace slows down.

The jjmath repository also contains quite a lot of formalized mathematics, the heaviest result at the moment being the uniformization theorem for simply-connected Riemann surfaces. (I also added a comparator challenge for that particular result, since its statement is actually quite close to Mathlib - one still had to define what is the complex structure on the Riemann sphere, though.)

This repository is mainly meant for my own private use, is in a quite messy state at the moment, and I'm not really looking for contributions. However I'm always happy to hear comments, and you are also totally free to copy from there as much as you like as well.

Finally, I'll also attach to this post a short essay I wrote on my experiences when working on this project so far. It also contains some not too carefully thought out thoughts on autoformalization and how it could look like in the future. I guess I hope that this could lead to others sharing their setups in a bit more detail as well, and perhaps also initiates some discussion on what mathematics and formalization might look like when autoformalization is done at scale. (Since I'm kind of coming from outside the community I'd also be happy to hear about pointers to existing discussions on these topics.)

handwave.pdf

That is very interesting, thanks for sharing. Can you add some screenshots to the handwave repo? I am curious, but installing a vscode repo just to see it in action is a bit of high bar.

perhaps also initiates some discussion on what mathematics and formalization might look like when autoformalization is done at scale

I am also very curious what starts to shape up as many people are building up similarly sized personal libraries of autoformalized results (I have the https://github.com/rkirov/jacobian-fable and https://github.com/rkirov/jordan_pick which now has almost all of uniformization too). It is pretty easy to for a single person to produce 50-100k loc of autoformalized lean a month on a Max Claude/GPT subscription. Which means if there are 100 people in the world doing that there will be 5-10 times the amount of math in mathlib randomly over github by the end of the year, with all the caveats - lower quality, duplicated, but still I believe of some reuse value mostly for further autoformalizations.

I guess https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool is one answer, but I am not sure the centralized model makes sense for this unlike mathlib. Pulling a whole multi GB repo with currently 1.5h build (is it possible to have mathlib style cache for random projects?) just for a few dependencies feels like a high cost, for the tradeoff of the quality/correctness/freshness guarantees the project provides.

There is room for something to help with just discovery of existing autoformalizations. I just looked at https://reservoir.lean-lang.org/ but it looks it hasn't accepted basic PRs for adding new projects recently (like https://github.com/leanprover/reservoir/issues/103).

Hi Janne, nice write up. This line grabbed my attention:

Apart from guides and getting people on board, I think one of the main missing pieces is a common social platform for sharing formalized mathematics

I think phrasing it as a "social media" platform is interesting. I think social media has many issues—fake news, bias, unsolicited advertising—but it also can be a powerful source of democratized information.

In a sense, this Zulip is one such platform. Github is another. Rado listed several "library" repos above which serve a similar purpose, as do journals like the Annals of Formalized Mathematics.

While there have been many attempts to standardize the autoformaliztion movement--projects today remain fragmented and isolated from each other. Relevant xkcd. Like many coding communities, one finds that the natural state of the internet is anarchy.

Rado Kirov said:

(is it possible to have mathlib style cache for random projects?)

AFAIK yeah (copy Mathlib's cache script) but you need to roll your own cloud storage. Also lake cache is in-the-works for any Lean project, not sure how that'll work but presumably you'll also need your own cloud storage.

Rado Kirov said:

I just looked at https://reservoir.lean-lang.org/ but it looks it hasn't accepted basic PRs for adding new projects recently

That's not how Reservoir works, it adds projects automatically; see https://reservoir.lean-lang.org/inclusion-criteria

Ah apologies, that makes sense. I wonder if the maintainers are interested in evolving it to support more features like formalization.yaml (getting off-topic for the original thread)

Rado Kirov said:

That is very interesting, thanks for sharing. Can you add some screenshots to the handwave repo? I am curious, but installing a vscode repo just to see it in action is a bit of high bar.

Excellent point, I actually had this in mind at some point but forgot. I have now added a couple of screenshots to the Handwave repository Also thanks for the links to your repositories, I had noticed your work on Jacobian challenge but did not know about the other one. It looks nice and maybe something I could try to learn from organization wise!

Those looks very nice, will give it a spin at some point.

It looks nice and maybe something I could try to learn from organization wise!

More likely the other way, I can learn from your project, since I have not put much effort into organization yet, but I enjoy sharing these efforts and cross-polinating good practices without big central push defining super concretely how should autoformalization projects look like (because at this point I think it is hard to tell what would that be). One more project that Fable finished in 5 days - https://github.com/rkirov/ClassificationOfFiniteSubgroupsOfPGL (on top of @Alex Brodbelt 's work, turns out FLT already got this independently in their slop folder).

I'd like to share a small update on Handwave, also related to Rado Kirov's comment on the VS Code dependency.

Handwave now has three operating modes:

  • The original VS Code extension.
  • A wiki-like webserver that you can point to your Lean/Handwave repository and view and edit the Handwave articles and metadata as well as browser theorems and definitions. This can be used as a replacement of the VS Code extension if desired.
  • A read-only static website generator version of the above. There is now also a demo of this at jjmath-demo.

See the GitHub repository for details.

(In addition JJMath itself has seen a bunch of additions, most notably the measurable Riemann mapping theorem and de Rham cohomology vs. singular cohomology equivalence, as well as some cleanup.)
